boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Mansfield (Sabine Cross-Roads) record (April 8, 1864) in the Red River Campaign [March-April 1864]. The April 7 cavalry fight at Wilson's farm and Carroll's mill and the Pleasant Hill battle of April 9 are context. Campaign-wide marches, returns, river operations and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Banks's Red River Expeditionary Force [US] and District of West Louisiana (two divisions) [CS]; the live field reads zero, and NPS says Taylor attacked though outnumbered. Irwin puts Ransom's infantry on the field at about 2,400, Banks's fighting line below 3,500 and the force at hand not above 5,000, against nearly 10,000 advancing under Taylor; Cameron's division barely 1,300; and Emory's division five thousand against a force half as large again. He says Taylor had at least sixteen thousand including Churchill's and Parsons's divisions, which Taylor says numbered about 4,000 bayonets and were ordered up from 20 miles away that morning. Irwin summarizes the Union as outnumbered almost two to one.
claims.rationale: Retrospective estimates by a Union staff officer for different phases and an interested report; the reinforcing divisions are not shown on the field on April 8. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Taylor says his line stood in the edge of a wood with cleared fields about 1,000 yards across on both sides of the Pleasant Hill road, in wooded country offering no field for many guns. Irwin describes the clearing as barely half a mile wide in a wilderness of pines, Taylor's position covering the crossing of the roads to Pleasant Hill, Shreveport, Bayou Pierre and the Sabine, and the Union column strung on a single narrow road. NPS places the position just below Mansfield near Sabine Cross-Roads.
claims.rationale: Ground described by an interested report, a history and a summary; no map verification. Taylor chose the position, so it is not tagged inherited.

claims.value: Taylor says he ordered Mouton to open the attack and that the left-wing movements were under Green's immediate direction; Irwin says it is not clear whether Taylor ordered Mouton's attack or Mouton attacked without his orders. Irwin says Banks rode to the extreme front, that his staff's direct action sandwiched Ransom's regiments, and that Emory's division, formed under Emory's orders, checked the pursuit. The frozen commanders are Major Generals Richard Taylor and Nathaniel P. Banks, as on the live page.
claims.rationale: Command roles from an interested report and a history; the opening of the attack is disputed, and the listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Confederate victory and the live result Confederate Victory. Taylor's order calls it the most complete victory in war and his report says his men camped on the creek with the enemy forced back some 400 yards; Irwin says Emory's twenty-minute fight rolled back the pursuit, and NPS that a third Union division halted the attack after more than an hour.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The final phase at the creek is described differently.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 4,400 total (US 2,900; CS 1,500); the live field reads 3235 (US 2235; CS 1000). Irwin's table gives Banks's loss as 115 killed, 648 wounded and 1,423 missing, 2,186 in all, and says Taylor put his own loss at 1,000; twenty Union guns were lost. Taylor's April 11 order claims twenty-one guns, 2,500 prisoners and 250 wagons; his report says the consolidated casualty report for the two battles was not found and that the cavalry would swell the whole loss to 2,500. Irwin's appendix says the War Department could not separate the losses of April 8 and 9.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. The two-day totals belong to both LA018 and LA019 and are not split or added.

open_questions: Banks's report (No. 2), Franklin's, Ransom's, Cameron's, Landram's, Lee's, Emory's and the regimental reports (Nos. 7-29, 60, 68-74, 81-88), Kirby Smith's report and correspondence (No. 93), Walker's and Green's reports, the No. 1 return abstract and the consolidated Confederate casualty report (not found in the OR) remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Richard B. Irwin's History of the Nineteenth Army Corps (Putnam's, 1892) is a retrospective history by the former assistant adjutant-general of the corps and of Banks's Department of the Gulf, an interested Union account; it cites the Official Records and gives Taylor's and Kirby Smith's figures, so it is not independent of them. Taylor's April 18, 1864 report, his March 13-14 letters printed as its inclosures, his April 24-May 19 dispatches and his April 11 general order are one family of interested Confederate accounts. Official Records Series I, Volume XXXIV, Part 1 is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
